message:
feat(update): the credential goes to one origin, and the shape comes from the url

Two C++ consumers were reading two different contracts off the same route.
The UI check read the server's one-object answer; the elevated worker asked
for manifestUrl + ".sig". On a derived url that appends to a query string --
...?platform=windows.sig -- an address the server has never served. The same
defect as the Android one fixed last round, and invisible for the same
reason: the url only ever came from an environment variable, so that line
had never run against the real server.

The detached shape is not wrong, though. A static host really does publish
two files. So neither shape is guessed from the response -- a truncated
answer of one kind looks like a valid answer of the other -- and the kind
travels with the url: derived means envelope, an explicit override means
detached, and the worker is told which with a flag rather than left to work
it out.

The route needs a session or a host token, so a derived url has to carry
one. UpdateEndpoint is a snapshot -- url, kind, credential, the one origin
it may reach, and the owner it belongs to -- because reading the url back
out of global state later and deciding *then* whether to attach a credential
is where this goes wrong: between the decision and the send, the account can
change and so can the server address.

An override never carries one, even pointed at our own host. What decides is
where the url came from, not what it looks like; a rule about what it looks
like is a comparison, and a comparison can be wrong on the day it matters.
Every destination is judged separately, including each artifact the manifest
names -- a signature over a manifest says its bytes are the right bytes, not
that our directory's credential belongs to whoever hosts them. And a request
carrying a credential follows no redirect at all: refusing https-to-http is
not enough when https://elsewhere is still https.

url_origin and update_endpoint are new files because the product and the
updater are deliberately separate trees. Without somewhere shared, origin
normalisation would be written twice, and the two copies would disagree
about a trailing slash or a written-out default port -- the same split this
repository already had in its scheme test.

What is NOT verified: the headers were never observed on the wire. That
needs a certificate the machine trusts, which is the same wall the redirect
regression is behind; a self-signed fixture breaks before any header is
sent. What is asserted is the decision -- fifteen cases across both
runtimes -- and "the gate is right" is not "the gate held".

Also red before this and now fixed: updater_assembly_test asserted the
installed version came from the manifest and not from kProductVersion, with
the fixture pinned to 0.2.105. The build was bumped to 0.2.105 in 9ff1716,
so the two became equal and the assertion could no longer be true. It is
99.0.0 now, which cannot ever be a release number. A literal chasing a
moving value is green while it happens to differ and checks nothing.
